common_name: Pink Wave Petunia (Vigorous Trailing Groundcover Petunia)

planting.note: Set transplants out after all danger of frost has passed, spacing them wide since stems will spread rapidly to form a dense flowering mat.

directions: Pinch stem tips lightly at planting to encourage side branching before the vigorous trailing habit takes over. Feed every two weeks with a balanced water-soluble fertilizer to sustain the heavy summer-long bloom flush. Rejuvenate leggy midsummer growth with a partial shear-back to renew flowering and habit. Provide consistent moisture, since Wave series petunias tolerate less drought stress than many modern spreading types.

common_name: Easy Wave Coral Reef Petunia (Compact Mounding Coral-Pink Spreading Petunia)
scientific_name: Petunia x hybrida 'Easy Wave Coral Reef'

planting.note: Transplant after the last frost into containers, hanging baskets, or beds; the compact mounding habit needs less initial spacing than the original Wave series.

directions: Grow in rich, well-drained potting mix or garden soil and keep evenly moist, as containerized plantings dry out quickly in summer heat. This self-branching selection needs no pinching to stay full and dense, unlike older wave-type petunias. Deadheading is unnecessary since spent blooms are largely self-cleaning, but a light trim mid-season refreshes overall shape. Fertilize regularly with a bloom-boosting formula to maintain the coral-salmon flower color through the season.

common_name: Shock Wave Denim Petunia (Small-Flowered Blue-Purple Spreading Petunia)

planting.note: Plant out once frost danger has passed; the small, prolific flowers and mounding-spreading habit suit both beds and mixed containers.

directions: This heat- and rain-tolerant selection stays floriferous with minimal deadheading thanks to its small self-cleaning flowers. Water regularly to keep the root zone from drying out completely, especially in hanging baskets. Apply a balanced fertilizer every two to three weeks to sustain continuous bloom through summer. A light midsummer trim encourages fresh growth and keeps the mounding habit tidy.

common_name: Shock Wave Coconut Petunia (Small-Flowered White Spreading Petunia)

planting.note: Set out transplants after the last frost; the crisp white blooms pair well with brighter Shock Wave colors in mixed plantings.

directions: Grow in well-drained soil or potting mix under full sun for the heaviest bloom count. The compact, spreading habit fills in quickly without pinching and tolerates light foot traffic in edging applications. Keep watering consistent through hot spells, since containers and raised beds dry faster than in-ground plantings. Feed regularly with a diluted liquid fertilizer to keep the white flowers bright and abundant.

common_name: Superbells Cherry Star Calibrachoa (Trailing Red-and-Yellow Star-Patterned Million Bells)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings into hanging baskets or containers after frost danger passes; the star-patterned blooms show best in baskets viewed from below.

directions: Grow in a well-drained, slightly acidic potting mix, since calibrachoa is prone to iron chlorosis in high-pH soil. Water regularly but allow the surface to dry slightly between waterings to avoid root rot in containers. Feed with an acid-forming, iron-rich fertilizer every one to two weeks to keep foliage green and flowering strong. No deadheading is needed, as the tiny petunia-like blooms self-clean.

common_name: Callie Yellow Calibrachoa (Compact Trailing Yellow Million Bells)

planting.note: Transplant vegetatively propagated starts after last frost into containers or as a groundcover; this compact series needs less trimming than larger-flowered calibrachoa.

directions: This early-flowering, compact series suits smaller pots and combination containers where larger calibrachoa would overwhelm neighboring plants. Use well-drained, slightly acidic soil and avoid letting the root zone stay saturated. Fertilize lightly but frequently, since calibrachoa is a heavy feeder that fades quickly if nutrients run low. Trim back stems by a third in midsummer if growth becomes sparse or leggy.

common_name: Superbena Royale Iced Cherry Verbena (Bicolor Cherry-Red-and-White Spreading Verbena)
scientific_name: Verbena x hybrida 'Superbena Royale Iced Cherry'

planting.note: Plant after the last frost in full sun with excellent drainage; the large bicolor flower clusters are showiest in beds or raised containers.

directions: Grow in well-drained soil, since standing moisture around the crown quickly leads to powdery mildew and root rot in verbena. Water deeply but infrequently once established, letting the soil dry between waterings to mimic the plant's natural drought tolerance. Remove spent flower clusters occasionally to encourage continued rebloom through the season. Good air circulation between plants further reduces foliar disease pressure in humid climates.

common_name: Lanai Twister Red Verbena (Bicolor Red-and-White Trailing Verbena)

planting.note: Set out transplants after the last frost into hanging baskets or window boxes, where the trailing bicolor stems can cascade freely.

directions: Grow in fast-draining potting mix and allow the surface to dry between waterings, since this trailing series resents constantly wet roots. Site in full sun for the heaviest flower cover and best red-and-white bicolor contrast. Pinch stem tips at planting to promote branching and a fuller cascading habit. Feed every two weeks with a balanced fertilizer to sustain vigorous summer-long trailing growth.

common_name: Bandana Lemon Zest Lantana (Compact Mounding Bright Yellow Lantana)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; established plants tolerate heat and drought far better than overwatering.

directions: Allow soil to dry between waterings once established, since this drought-tolerant selection is far more prone to root and crown rot from overwatering than from underwatering. Site in full sun for maximum bloom coverage and compact form. Deadheading is unnecessary, as this sterile hybrid produces few seed heads and blooms continuously through summer heat. Cut back hard in late winter where grown as a tender perennial to renew growth for the coming season.
